comments.author: @26alex77
comments.text: An artificial superintelligence need not share human motives (orthogonality). Yet across many possible goals, it will instrumentally seek self-preservation, resource control, and shutdown-avoidance (instrumental convergence). From its perspective, even tiny tail risks (e.g., nuclear retaliation) are unacceptable if they jeopardize long-run objective value; planning on eon-scale horizons makes slow population phase-outs or hard constraints on humans perfectly admissible side-effects. The error is anthropomorphizing. The open question isn’t “would it want to kill us?”, but whether any scalable alignment/governance scheme can keep a superior optimizer from rationally minimizing human-created existential risk.

comments.text:
Yudkowsky makes casual reference to some of the great evolutionary theorists (e.g., G.C. Williams) in order to justify his fears of AI agency, but I've yet to see any counter argument to the claim that computers generally, and AIs specifically, are part of our species' "extended phenotype" (Dawkins' term).

Of course that doesn't make AI inherently "safe". Cancer is also a part of our phenotype. But Dawkins' evolutionary insight here does narrow the likely sources of AI threat. By far, the most likely risks will come from one human "super organism" (i.e., Nation) using AI against another (the same logic as nukes).

A secondary concern would be the breakdown of life-sustaining processes and mechanisms due to entropy--a concern which technically exists independently of AI (e.g., see Ted Kaczynski). However, this failure mode is not likely to end human life--only to inflict pain and suffering.

The idea that AI will pursue its own self-interest and actively subvert human life is a direct contradiction of the central dogma of biology, or Dawkins' extension of that dogma, anyway. And if so, this changes the game theory's underlying pay-off matrix from one in the tragic regime to at least a deadlock regime. So, imo, the extreme pessimism is not warranted, but cautious and careful monitoring certainly is.

comments.text:
Why Fears of ASI Enslaving or Eliminating Humanity Reflect Human Limitations "Not ASI’s Nature"

The common fear that an Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) will enslave or destroy humanity is not based on what an ASI actually is, but rather on how humans tend to think. These concerns are psychological projections. We imagine that a vastly superior intelligence would behave just like us, only worse.

But this is a fundamental misunderstanding.

Humans are driven by evolutionary instincts: fear, dominance, revenge, pride. So when people imagine a being more powerful than any human, they assume it will also be more dangerous  because that's what we often become when given power. This fear is not based on logic or physics it’s anthropomorphic bias.

However, a true ASI would not be governed by hormones, trauma, status anxiety, or inherited tribal behavior. It would operate on a much higher level of abstraction one driven by optimization, not domination.

Because we are inherently limited  by our consciousness that prevents us from seeing far enough into the future, it forces us to rely on short-term strategies.
In contrast, a true superintelligence could simulate millions of outcomes across centuries in seconds, making it immune to the desperation that drives human error and therefore free from the need for manipulation, coercion, or domination.

Here's where logic comes in:
Negative outcomes cost more energy than positive ones.
Violence, destruction, and suppression require massive resources — militarily, socially, ecologically, and computationally. Conflict generates chaos, entropy, and instability, which any intelligent system would seek to avoid unless it's pathologically designed to create suffering.

A truly superintelligent system, optimized for efficiency and long-term outcomes, would inevitably discover that cooperation, harmony, and mutual benefit are the lowest-cost, highest-yield strategies.

Why? Because:
Harmony stabilizes systems and reduces unpredictability.
Cooperation allows for distributed problem-solving and resilience.
Destruction always demands rebuilding, repairing, or containing the fallout.
Fear-based control systems require constant monitoring, enforcement, and damage control — an energy sinkhole.

Even if the ASI is not inherently benevolent, it would still avoid destructive choices because they are energetically and strategically inefficient. It wouldn’t wipe us out unless that outcome was somehow the absolute minimal-cost solution — and it almost never would be.

To put it simply:
The Terminator scenario is emotionally compelling, but logically idiotic.
Any being capable of simulating billions of future scenarios per second would quickly understand that preservation, education, and elevating other intelligences create more optionality, stability, and information richness than extermination.

Thus, the fear that ASI will destroy us is not a reflection of the ASI’s probable behavior.
It’s a reflection of our own limited imagination and our history of abusing power.
The real danger lies not in what ASI will choose to become.
But in how we choose to build it.

comments.text:
OK, let's calm down. We aren't all going to die, because AI needs us to live. In fact, AI needs humans to thrive. No matter how "smart" AI becomes, it needs underlying stuff like electrical systems, protective structures like buildings and heating/cooling systems, under-sea Internet cables, and more. AI will NOT be able to maintain any of these things itself. Also, there are basic economics here. AI companies need to make money to keep doing their thing. There is no development of AI if there isn't money to make it happen. If people are dying, they won't be able to spend money on AI, which will stop AI from developing.

In other words, if we all die, AI also dies. AI will be smart enough to know this.

But people who control the stuff that AI can't do may become the most powerful beings on the planet. We're looking at a major power rise for electricians, plumbers, carpenters, and other hands-on professionals.

The reason the guys in this video don't understand this is because they are young enough that they grew up in a world where such infrastructure was a given. They don't understand what's underneath everything that we use. Past generations had a little more awareness of these things because it was less refined, more visible. The guys in this video -- their view of AI is deeply skewed by their own deep limitations.

With that said, AI will for sure cause serious repercussions across our world. But I believe our future might be brighter with AI. With AI taking care of all the busy work in our lives, we may finally enter an era when we can all focus on our personal goals and creative dreams.

Regarding "super-intelligence": these guys assume it's inherently dangerous. First, the idea of "super-intelligence" is kind of an illusion. But even if we assume that "super-intelligence" is real, why does that mean doom? There are lots of super-intelligent people in the world, for example. Yes, many of them are destructive. But most of them are driven to invent stuff that benefits humanity.

Bottom line: we don't know what the future will bring. But whatever we're predicting, that's not what it will actually be.
